meaning: Learn how to do or use something through practice.
easyEnglish: Learn how to do or use something through practice.
japanese: 練習を通じて、やり方やこつをつかむ。
cue: Describe gradually learning to use a new camera.
reply: I'm starting to get the hang of this camera.
transferCue: Reassure a friend learning a card game.
transferReply: You'll get the hang of the rules after a couple of rounds.
frame: Get the hang of something / doing something
nuance: Informal; follow of with a noun or an -ing form.

phrase: get the wrong end of the stick
meaning: Misunderstand what someone means or what a situation is.
easyEnglish: Misunderstand what someone means or what a situation is.
japanese: 話や状況を勘違いする。
cue: Correct your mistaken interpretation of a dinner invitation.
reply: I got the wrong end of the stick; I thought dinner was at your place.
transferCue: Explain why a colleague wrongly expected a cancellation.
transferReply: He got the wrong end of the stick when I mentioned changing the date.
frame: Get the wrong end of the stick
nuance: Especially British English; often useful when acknowledging your own misunderstanding.

meaning: Organize yourself so you behave or work more effectively.
easyEnglish: Organize yourself so you behave or work more effectively.
japanese: 行動や準備をきちんと整え、しっかりやる。
cue: Give firm advice to a teammate who repeatedly arrives unprepared.
reply: You need to get your act together before the client visit.
transferCue: Encourage a friend to organize overdue applications.
transferReply: If you get your act together this weekend, you can submit everything on Monday.
frame: Get your act together
nuance: Informal and potentially critical; use a gentler alternative when someone needs support.

meaning: Try something, even if you are unsure it will work.
easyEnglish: Try something, even if you are unsure it will work.
japanese: うまくいくか分からなくても、ひとまず試す。
cue: Encourage a friend to try an unfamiliar class.
reply: The pottery class looks fun; why not give it a shot?
transferCue: Agree to attempt a repair before replacing an item.
transferReply: I've never fixed a chair before, but I'll give it a shot.
frame: Give it a shot
nuance: Informal; give it a try is a neutral alternative.

meaning: Return to the simplest, most important principles.
easyEnglish: Return to the simplest, most important principles.
japanese: 基本に立ち返る。
cue: Suggest simplifying an overcomplicated design.
reply: Let's go back to basics and ask what the user actually needs.
transferCue: Recommend revisiting fundamental skills after repeated mistakes.
transferReply: I decided to go back to basics and practice simple chords.
frame: Go back to basics
nuance: Used when complexity or lost focus makes the fundamental approach useful again.

meaning: Fail completely, often in a noticeable or dramatic way.
easyEnglish: Fail completely, often in a noticeable or dramatic way.
japanese: 大きく、はっきりと失敗する。
cue: Describe a proposal rejected by everyone at a meeting.
reply: Our proposal went down in flames when nobody supported it.
transferCue: Explain the collapse of an ambitious competition plan.
transferReply: The plan to enter every event went down in flames after the first day.
frame: Go down in flames
nuance: Informal and dramatic; for modest setbacks, failed may be more proportionate.

meaning: Accept developments and adapt instead of insisting on a fixed plan.
easyEnglish: Accept developments and adapt instead of insisting on a fixed plan.
japanese: 流れに逆らわず、状況に合わせる。
cue: Explain your relaxed approach to a weekend trip.
reply: We haven't booked every hour; we'll just go with the flow.
transferCue: Encourage a friend to adapt when dinner plans change.
transferReply: Let's go with the flow and join them at the new restaurant.
frame: Go with the flow
nuance: Usually suggests flexibility; it can also imply following others without much independent choice.

phrase: have a lot on your plate
meaning: Have many tasks or responsibilities to deal with.
easyEnglish: Have many tasks or responsibilities to deal with.
japanese: やることや抱えている責任がたくさんある。
cue: Acknowledge that a friend is already very busy.
reply: You have a lot on your plate, so I can handle the shopping.
transferCue: Suggest declining extra work during a demanding week.
transferReply: You already have a lot on your plate without organizing the event too.
frame: Have a lot on your plate
nuance: Informal; the plate represents responsibilities, not food in these contexts.

meaning: Have more important matters to deal with.
easyEnglish: Have more important matters to deal with.
japanese: もっと重要な用事や問題がある。
cue: Explain why you are leaving a minor disagreement alone.
reply: I have bigger fish to fry than arguing about the poster color.
transferCue: Say that your team must focus on a more important task.
transferReply: We have bigger fish to fry with the opening only a week away.
frame: Have bigger fish to fry than doing something
nuance: Informal; can sound dismissive of the smaller issue or the people concerned.

meaning: Start doubting a decision you previously made.
easyEnglish: Start doubting a decision you previously made.
japanese: 一度決めたことを、考え直したり迷い始めたりする。
cue: Explain that you are reconsidering a house move.
reply: I'm starting to have second thoughts about moving so far away.
transferCue: Ask a friend whether they still want to run an event.
transferReply: Do you have second thoughts about hosting the workshop?
frame: Have second thoughts about something / doing something
nuance: Usually plural thoughts; it signals doubt, not necessarily a final change of decision.

meaning: Deeply in love or extremely enthusiastic about someone.
easyEnglish: Deeply in love or extremely enthusiastic about someone.
japanese: すっかり恋に落ちて、夢中になって。
cue: Describe a friend's feelings for their new partner.
reply: She's head over heels in love with her new partner.
transferCue: Explain why someone keeps talking about their date.
transferReply: He's clearly head over heels; he hasn't stopped smiling all morning.
frame: Be head over heels in love with someone
nuance: Informal; these examples teach the romantic sense, not a literal tumble.

meaning: Reach an obstacle that stops further progress.
easyEnglish: Reach an obstacle that stops further progress.
japanese: 行き詰まり、先へ進めなくなる。
cue: Explain why a permit application has stopped progressing.
reply: We've hit a brick wall with the permit application.
transferCue: Describe getting stuck in your family history research.
transferReply: I hit a brick wall when the records stopped at 1890.
frame: Hit a brick wall with something
nuance: Also hit a wall; it marks a serious obstacle rather than ordinary slow progress.

meaning: Begin studying seriously.
easyEnglish: Begin studying seriously.
japanese: 本格的に勉強に取りかかる。
cue: Tell a friend you need to study instead of going out.
reply: I'd love to join you, but I need to hit the books tonight.
transferCue: Describe preparing for an important certification exam.
transferReply: She's hitting the books every evening before the exam.
frame: Hit the books
nuance: Informal; refers to studying even when the materials are digital.

meaning: Start a new activity effectively with little delay.
easyEnglish: Start a new activity effectively with little delay.
japanese: 新しいことを始めてすぐ、順調に力を発揮する。
cue: Explain why preparation helped a new colleague.
reply: With the handover notes ready, she could hit the ground running.
transferCue: Describe preparing before volunteering at a festival.
transferReply: We practiced the system so we could hit the ground running on opening day.
frame: Hit the ground running
nuance: Often used when starting a job or project; it emphasizes a strong start.

meaning: Leave to begin a journey.
easyEnglish: Leave to begin a journey.
japanese: 出発する、旅に出る。
cue: Suggest leaving before the traffic gets heavy.
reply: Let's hit the road before the rush starts.
transferCue: Tell your hosts that it is time to leave.
transferReply: Thanks for lunch; we'd better hit the road now.
frame: Hit the road
nuance: Informal. As a bare command, hit the road can sound like telling someone to go away.

meaning: Go to bed.
easyEnglish: Go to bed.
japanese: 寝る、床に就く。
cue: Say you are going to bed after a tiring day.
reply: I'm exhausted, so I'm going to hit the sack.
transferCue: Explain an early night before a morning flight.
transferReply: We should hit the sack soon; the taxi comes at five.
frame: Hit the sack
nuance: Very informal; hit the hay is another casual expression with the same meaning.

meaning: Wait or slow down before taking action.
easyEnglish: Wait or slow down before taking action.
japanese: ちょっと待つ、焦らず落ち着く。
cue: Stop a friend from leaving before everyone is ready.
reply: Hold your horses! We haven't packed the picnic yet.
transferCue: Ask a teammate not to announce an unconfirmed result.
transferReply: Hold your horses; we still need to check the final numbers.
frame: Hold your horses!
nuance: Informal and sometimes old-fashioned or playful; it can sound patronizing in a serious discussion.

meaning: Expressed briefly, using only the main points.
easyEnglish: Expressed briefly, using only the main points.
japanese: 要点だけを短く言うと。
cue: Summarize a proposal in one sentence.
reply: In a nutshell, we need more time and a smaller launch.
transferCue: Explain the central idea of a film without details.
transferReply: It's about two strangers learning to trust each other, in a nutshell.
frame: In a nutshell, …
nuance: Useful before a short summary; a long explanation afterward defeats its purpose.

meaning: At a very active or busy stage.
easyEnglish: At a very active or busy stage.
japanese: 物事が盛んに進んでいる、真っ最中で。
cue: Describe arriving after a party had become lively.
reply: The party was in full swing when we arrived.
transferCue: Explain the current stage of preparations.
transferReply: Preparations for the festival are in full swing.
frame: Be in full swing
nuance: Describes an activity underway with energy, not something that has merely started.

phrase: in the blink of an eye
meaning: Extremely quickly.
easyEnglish: Extremely quickly.
japanese: あっという間に、瞬く間に。
cue: Describe how quickly tickets disappeared.
reply: The tickets sold out in the blink of an eye.
transferCue: Explain how suddenly a quiet square became crowded.
transferReply: The square filled with people in the blink of an eye.
frame: Happen in the blink of an eye
nuance: Usually exaggeration for speed; it is not an exact measure of time.

meaning: Without important information about something.
easyEnglish: Without important information about something.
japanese: 大事な事情を知らされず、分からないままで。
cue: Ask to be kept informed about a project change.
reply: Please don't leave us in the dark about the new schedule.
transferCue: Explain that your friend has not heard the travel plans.
transferReply: He's still in the dark about where we're going.
frame: Be / keep someone in the dark about something
nuance: This figurative use concerns missing information; literal darkness is a separate sense.

meaning: In control of a situation or its decisions.
easyEnglish: In control of a situation or its decisions.
japanese: 状況を主導し、決定権を持っている。
cue: Explain who now controls a project after a handover.
reply: With the handover complete, our team is in the driver's seat.
transferCue: Encourage a friend who can choose between several offers.
transferReply: With three offers to consider, you're in the driver's seat.
frame: Be / put someone in the driver's seat
nuance: Figurative control, not necessarily a formal management role.

meaning: Just before it would have been too late.
easyEnglish: Just before it would have been too late.
japanese: 手遅れになる直前の、ぎりぎりのタイミングで。
cue: Describe arriving moments before a gate closed.
reply: We reached the gate in the nick of time.
transferCue: Explain how a friend prevented food from burning.
transferReply: She took the bread out of the oven in the nick of time.
frame: Arrive / do something in the nick of time
nuance: Emphasizes narrowly avoiding being too late; not simply being punctual.

meaning: Two people are involved in, or share responsibility for, a situation.
easyEnglish: Two people are involved in, or share responsibility for, a situation.
japanese: ある状況やもめ事には、双方が関わっているということ。
cue: Acknowledge your part in an argument with a roommate.
reply: It takes two to tango; I interrupted you as well.
transferCue: Explain why cooperation needs effort from both teams.
transferReply: It takes two to tango, so both teams need to share information.
frame: It takes two to tango
nuance: Can concern conflict or cooperation; do not use it to assume blame is always equal.

meaning: Join an activity because it has become popular or successful.
easyEnglish: Join an activity because it has become popular or successful.
japanese: 流行や成功に乗じて、自分も参加する。
cue: Describe shops suddenly following the same decorating trend.
reply: Several cafes jumped on the bandwagon and painted everything pink.
transferCue: Explain why you want evidence before adopting a trend.
transferReply: I'd rather test the idea than jump on the bandwagon.
frame: Jump on the bandwagon
nuance: Often mildly critical, suggesting imitation rather than an independent choice.

meaning: Act before the right time or before having enough information.
easyEnglish: Act before the right time or before having enough information.
japanese: 時期尚早に行動する、早まる。
cue: Warn a friend against booking before dates are confirmed.
reply: Don't jump the gun and book flights before the dates are final.
transferCue: Apologize for announcing a decision too soon.
transferReply: I jumped the gun when I said the venue was confirmed.
frame: Jump the gun
nuance: Originally a racing image; here the mistake is acting too soon.

meaning: Avoid attracting attention to yourself.
easyEnglish: Avoid attracting attention to yourself.
japanese: 目立たないようにする。
cue: Explain why you avoided attention during a tense week.
reply: I decided to keep a low profile until things settled down.
transferCue: Describe a well-known visitor's quiet stay.
transferReply: The actor kept a low profile during her visit to the island.
frame: Keep a low profile
nuance: Can be strategic or personal; it does not necessarily mean hiding wrongdoing.

meaning: Be willing to consider new ideas before deciding.
easyEnglish: Be willing to consider new ideas before deciding.
japanese: 決めつけず、新しい考えや可能性を受け入れる姿勢を持つ。
cue: Encourage a friend to try an unfamiliar kind of music.
reply: Keep an open mind; you might enjoy the live performance.
transferCue: Explain how you will assess an unusual proposal.
transferReply: I'll keep an open mind until I've heard the details.
frame: Keep an open mind about something
nuance: Willingness to consider an idea does not require agreeing with it.

meaning: Stay hopeful during a difficult time.
easyEnglish: Stay hopeful during a difficult time.
japanese: つらい時も元気を出して、前向きでいる。
cue: Encourage a friend after a disappointing audition.
reply: Keep your chin up; that audition doesn't define your talent.
transferCue: Support a teammate who is frustrated by slow progress.
transferReply: Keep your chin up. You've already improved more than you realize.
frame: Keep your chin up
nuance: Informal encouragement; acknowledge the difficulty so it does not sound dismissive.

meaning: Hope that something will turn out well.
easyEnglish: Hope that something will turn out well.
japanese: うまくいくようにと願う。
cue: Ask a friend to hope your application succeeds.
reply: Keep your fingers crossed for me; the results come tomorrow.
transferCue: Ask others to hope the weather stays suitable.
transferReply: Keep your fingers crossed that the rain holds off until evening.
frame: Keep your fingers crossed for someone / that…
nuance: Expresses hope rather than certainty; fingers crossed can stand alone as a shorter wish.

meaning: Manage to cope with a difficult situation, especially money or work.
easyEnglish: Manage to cope with a difficult situation, especially money or work.
japanese: 仕事やお金などの苦しい状況で、何とか持ちこたえる。
cue: Acknowledge a friend's effort during a demanding month.
reply: You're doing well to keep your head above water with everything going on.
transferCue: Encourage someone managing a tight household budget.
transferReply: Cutting that regular fee could help you keep your head above water.
frame: Keep your head above water
nuance: Suggests coping with little spare capacity, rather than thriving or getting ahead.

meaning: Avoid committing too soon so other choices remain possible.
easyEnglish: Avoid committing too soon so other choices remain possible.
japanese: ほかの選択肢も残しておく。
cue: Advise a friend considering several courses.
reply: Apply to both schools to keep your options open.
transferCue: Suggest flexible arrangements for an uncertain trip.
transferReply: A refundable booking will help you keep your options open.
frame: Keep your options open
nuance: Usually concerns postponing commitment, not refusing to make any decision forever.

meaning: Do what you promised.
easyEnglish: Do what you promised.
japanese: 約束を守る。
cue: Thank a friend for following through on a promise.
reply: I appreciate that you always keep your word.
transferCue: Remind a teammate to honor an agreed deadline.
transferReply: If you promise Friday, please keep your word.
frame: Keep your word
nuance: Word is singular here; give your word means make a promise.

phrase: kill two birds with one stone
meaning: Achieve two useful things through a single action.
easyEnglish: Achieve two useful things through a single action.
japanese: 一つの行動で二つの目的を達成する。一石二鳥。
cue: Suggest combining exercise with an errand.
reply: We can kill two birds with one stone by walking to the post office.
transferCue: Explain why you arranged a visit near a work meeting.
transferReply: I'll kill two birds with one stone and visit my aunt after the meeting.
frame: Kill two birds with one stone by doing something
nuance: A figurative efficiency expression; the actions should serve two distinct purposes.

meaning: Learn the practical skills and procedures needed for an activity.
easyEnglish: Learn the practical skills and procedures needed for an activity.
japanese: 仕事や活動の基本的なやり方を覚える。
cue: Explain why a new volunteer needs guidance.
reply: She's still learning the ropes, so I'll stay nearby to help.
transferCue: Describe your first weeks running a market stall.
transferReply: It took a few weekends to learn the ropes at the market.
frame: Learn the ropes
nuance: Know the ropes means already understand the practical details; show someone the ropes means teach them.

meaning: Try every possible way to solve a problem or find something.
easyEnglish: Try every possible way to solve a problem or find something.
japanese: あらゆる手段を尽くす。
cue: Promise a thorough search for a lost file.
reply: We'll leave no stone unturned in trying to recover the missing file.
transferCue: Describe a neighborhood search for a missing pet.
transferReply: The neighbors left no stone unturned until the cat was found.
frame: Leave no stone unturned in doing something
nuance: Emphasizes thorough effort; avoid promising it when only a quick check is realistic.

meaning: Avoid raising an old issue that could cause trouble again.
easyEnglish: Avoid raising an old issue that could cause trouble again.
japanese: 蒸し返すと面倒になる問題に、あえて触れない。
cue: Suggest not reopening an old, settled disagreement.
reply: We've already apologized, so let's let sleeping dogs lie.
transferCue: Explain why you did not mention an old family argument.
transferReply: I decided to let sleeping dogs lie during the reunion.
frame: Let sleeping dogs lie
nuance: Advice to avoid renewed conflict; it is not appropriate for ignoring an unresolved urgent problem.

phrase: let the cat out of the bag
meaning: Reveal a secret, often accidentally.
easyEnglish: Reveal a secret, often accidentally.
japanese: 秘密をうっかり漏らす。
cue: Admit that you accidentally revealed a surprise trip.
reply: I let the cat out of the bag when I mentioned the flight.
transferCue: Warn a friend not to reveal an unannounced gift.
transferReply: Don't let the cat out of the bag before she opens the box.
frame: Let the cat out of the bag
nuance: Often accidental; similar to spill the beans, which can also describe deliberate disclosure.

phrase: light at the end of the tunnel
meaning: A sign that a difficult period may soon end.
easyEnglish: A sign that a difficult period may soon end.
japanese: 苦しい時期の終わりが見える希望。
cue: Describe hope as a long renovation nears completion.
reply: With the kitchen nearly finished, there's light at the end of the tunnel.
transferCue: Encourage a team nearing the end of a large backlog.
transferReply: The queue is finally shrinking; I can see light at the end of the tunnel.
frame: See light at the end of the tunnel
nuance: Suggests an approaching improvement after difficulty, rather than guaranteed success.

meaning: Something extremely difficult to find among many other things.
easyEnglish: Something extremely difficult to find among many other things.
japanese: 大量のものの中から見つけるのが、非常に難しい。
cue: Describe searching for a tiny earring on a crowded beach.
reply: That earring is like a needle in a haystack on this beach.
transferCue: Explain the difficulty of finding one unlabelled file.
transferReply: Finding that scan is like looking for a needle in a haystack.
frame: Be like / look for a needle in a haystack
nuance: The fuller comparison is like looking for a needle in a haystack.

meaning: Consider possible consequences before acting.
easyEnglish: Consider possible consequences before acting.
japanese: 行動する前に、結果や危険をよく考える。
cue: Advise a friend considering an unfamiliar rental agreement.
reply: Look before you leap; read the whole agreement before deciding.
transferCue: Encourage caution before joining a demanding volunteer role.
transferReply: It's exciting, but look before you leap and check the time commitment.
frame: Look before you leap
nuance: A proverb often used as advice; it promotes thought rather than avoiding all risks.

meaning: Forget the sequence of ideas you were about to express.
easyEnglish: Forget the sequence of ideas you were about to express.
japanese: 話そうとしていた考えの流れが途切れ、何を言うつもりだったか忘れる。
cue: Reassure a speaker after an interruption.
reply: Take your time if you lose your train of thought.
transferCue: Suggest silencing notifications before explaining a complex idea.
transferReply: Mute the alerts so you don't lose your train of thought.
frame: Lose your train of thought
nuance: Train of thought is the connected sequence of ideas, rather than one forgotten fact.

phrase: make a mountain out of a molehill
meaning: Treat a small problem as if it were much more serious.
easyEnglish: Treat a small problem as if it were much more serious.
japanese: 小さな問題を大げさに騒ぎ立てる。
cue: Admit that you overreacted to a minor typo.
reply: I made a mountain out of a molehill over one typo.
transferCue: Encourage yourself not to exaggerate a small delay.
transferReply: Let's not make a mountain out of a molehill; we're only five minutes late.
frame: Make a mountain out of a molehill
nuance: Can sound dismissive when directed at someone else's concern; useful for acknowledging your own overreaction.

meaning: Have enough money for necessary living costs.
easyEnglish: Have enough money for necessary living costs.
japanese: 生活に必要なお金を何とかまかなう。
cue: Explain why you took an extra shift last winter.
reply: I took extra shifts to make ends meet over the winter.
transferCue: Describe a household's difficulty after rent increased.
transferReply: With the higher rent, they're finding it hard to make ends meet.
frame: Struggle / manage to make ends meet
nuance: Concerns basic expenses, not saving for luxury purchases.

meaning: Attract attention by challenging normal ways or causing change.
easyEnglish: Attract attention by challenging normal ways or causing change.
japanese: 従来のやり方に異議を唱えるなどして、波紋を起こす。
cue: Explain why you hesitated to challenge an old process.
reply: I didn't want to make waves in my first week.
transferCue: Describe a new artist whose work is attracting attention.
transferReply: Her unusual performances are making waves in the local arts scene.
frame: Make waves in a group / field
nuance: Can be negative disruption or positive influence; the surrounding sentence establishes the tone.

meaning: News or words that make you very pleased.
easyEnglish: News or words that make you very pleased.
japanese: 聞いてとてもうれしい知らせや言葉。
cue: Tell a friend that a cancelled fee should please them.
reply: The waived delivery fee must be music to your ears.
transferCue: React to a teammate learning that help has arrived.
transferReply: Hearing that help is on the way must be music to your ears.
frame: Something is music to your ears
nuance: Change the possessive for the listener; this phrase describes welcome news, not actual music.

meaning: Without extra obligations or conditions.
easyEnglish: Without extra obligations or conditions.
japanese: 付帯条件や見返りの要求がなく。
cue: Offer a friend spare equipment without expecting repayment.
reply: You can have the spare desk, no strings attached.
transferCue: Clarify that a free workshop has no purchase requirement.
transferReply: The workshop is free with no strings attached.
frame: With no strings attached
nuance: Use only when there truly are no added obligations; strings metaphorically means conditions.

meaning: Not something I personally enjoy or find interesting.
easyEnglish: Not something I personally enjoy or find interesting.
japanese: 自分の好みではない。
cue: Politely explain why you do not enjoy horror films.
reply: Horror films are not my cup of tea, but enjoy the screening.
transferCue: Decline a noisy evening while respecting a friend's taste.
transferReply: Club nights are not my cup of tea; I'd love to meet for lunch instead.
frame: Something is not my cup of tea
nuance: A personal preference rather than an objective criticism; change my to match the speaker.

meaning: Not especially complicated or difficult to understand.
easyEnglish: Not especially complicated or difficult to understand.
japanese: それほど難しいことではない。
cue: Reassure yourself about learning a simple household task.
reply: Sorting the recycling is not rocket science once you know the colors.
transferCue: Encourage a team to try a straightforward process.
transferReply: The new check-in process is not rocket science; we'll practice it together.
frame: Something is not rocket science
nuance: Informal; saying it to someone who is struggling can sound condescending.

meaning: Away from places most people visit.
easyEnglish: Away from places most people visit.
japanese: 多くの人が訪れる場所から外れた、人里離れたところに。
cue: Recommend a quiet village away from busy tourist routes.
reply: That village is off the beaten track and perfect for a quiet weekend.
transferCue: Describe a small cafe you discovered while walking.
transferReply: We found a little cafe off the beaten track near the old canal.
frame: Be / go off the beaten track
nuance: Off the beaten path is a common alternative, especially in American English.

phrase: off the top of your head
meaning: From memory without checking or preparing.
easyEnglish: From memory without checking or preparing.
japanese: 調べたり準備したりせず、その場で思いつく範囲で。
cue: Ask for a rough estimate without requiring exact figures.
reply: Off the top of your head, how many people used the room last week?
transferCue: Ask a friend to recall a restaurant's name casually.
transferReply: Can you remember the name off the top of your head?
frame: Say / know something off the top of your head
nuance: Signals an unprepared answer, which may need checking before someone relies on it.

meaning: Having a continuing series of successes.
easyEnglish: Having a continuing series of successes.
japanese: 好調が続き、波に乗っている。
cue: Praise a teammate after several successful presentations.
reply: You're on a roll with these presentations.
transferCue: Describe a team's recent winning streak.
transferReply: The team is on a roll after winning four matches in a row.
frame: Be on a roll
nuance: Informal; suggests successive successes rather than one isolated achievement.

meaning: Extremely happy.
easyEnglish: Extremely happy.
japanese: とても幸せで、うきうきしている。
cue: Describe your reaction to being offered a place on a course.
reply: I was on cloud nine when the acceptance email arrived.
transferCue: Explain a friend's mood after a long-awaited reunion.
transferReply: She's been on cloud nine since seeing her sister again.
frame: Be on cloud nine
nuance: Informal and expressive; use for strong happiness rather than mild satisfaction.

meaning: Alert, quick to understand, and ready to act.
easyEnglish: Alert, quick to understand, and ready to act.
japanese: 状況を素早く理解し、てきぱき対応できる。
cue: Praise a colleague who noticed a booking mistake early.
reply: You were really on the ball to spot that booking error.
transferCue: Describe an organizer who handles changes promptly.
transferReply: Our coordinator is on the ball and answers every update quickly.
frame: Be on the ball
nuance: Informal praise for awareness and responsiveness, not physical movement.

meaning: Given less attention for now while other matters take priority.
easyEnglish: Given less attention for now while other matters take priority.
japanese: ほかを優先し、当面は後回しにして。
cue: Explain why a personal project is temporarily paused.
reply: The garden project is on the back burner until we fix the roof.
transferCue: Tell a team that a possible expansion will wait.
transferReply: We'll put expansion plans on the back burner this quarter.
frame: Put / keep something on the back burner
nuance: Usually a temporary lower priority, rather than a permanent cancellation.

meaning: Likely or possible to happen.
easyEnglish: Likely or possible to happen.
japanese: 起こる可能性がある、ありそうである。
cue: Say that an office move is a real possibility.
reply: An office move is on the cards for next year.
transferCue: Explain that a weekend trip might still happen.
transferReply: A short trip is still on the cards if the schedule works out.
frame: Something is on the cards
nuance: Mainly British English; American English usually uses in the cards.

meaning: Taking an approach that is likely to lead to the right result.
easyEnglish: Taking an approach that is likely to lead to the right result.
japanese: 正しい方向に進んでいる。
cue: Encourage a friend whose language practice is improving.
reply: Your conversations are getting smoother; you're on the right track.
transferCue: Give feedback on an unfinished proposal.
transferReply: The examples need work, but the overall idea is on the right track.
frame: Be on the right track
nuance: Signals useful progress, not that the work is complete or flawless.

meaning: In a risky position where another mistake could cause trouble.
easyEnglish: In a risky position where another mistake could cause trouble.
japanese: これ以上失敗すると困る、危うい立場にある。
cue: Describe a supplier's position after repeated missed deadlines.
reply: The supplier is on thin ice after missing two delivery dates.
transferCue: Warn a friend that repeated rule-breaking has consequences.
transferReply: You're on thin ice with the club after ignoring that warning.
frame: Be / skate on thin ice
nuance: Often concerns trust or permission that could soon be lost.

meaning: Impossible or not acceptable as an option.
easyEnglish: Impossible or not acceptable as an option.
japanese: 不可能、または選択肢として認められない。
cue: Explain that a proposed date cannot work.
reply: Traveling on Monday is out of the question; I have an exam.
transferCue: Set a firm limit on spending.
transferReply: A larger venue is out of the question with our current budget.
frame: Something is out of the question
nuance: Much stronger than unlikely; out of question without the has a different, uncommon use.

meaning: Past the worst part of a problem or danger.
easyEnglish: Past the worst part of a problem or danger.
japanese: 問題や危険の最も大変な段階を抜けて。
cue: Explain that a repaired service still needs monitoring.
reply: The service is running again, but we're not out of the woods yet.
transferCue: Describe cautiously improving finances for a club.
transferReply: Ticket sales are improving, though we're not out of the woods.
frame: Be out of the woods
nuance: Frequently negative with yet; it means the main danger has passed, not that every detail is solved.

meaning: Extremely pleased about something.
easyEnglish: Extremely pleased about something.
japanese: 何かがうれしくてたまらない。
cue: Describe receiving an unexpected invitation.
reply: I'm over the moon about the invitation to exhibit my work.
transferCue: Tell a friend how your parents reacted to good news.
transferReply: My parents were over the moon when I told them about the scholarship.
frame: Be over the moon about something
nuance: Especially common in British English; expresses strong delight.

meaning: Shift responsibility or blame to someone else.
easyEnglish: Shift responsibility or blame to someone else.
japanese: 責任や非難をほかの人に押しつける。
cue: Ask a team to stop shifting responsibility for an error.
reply: Let's fix the issue instead of passing the buck.
transferCue: Describe being sent between departments without help.
transferReply: Each department passed the buck to the next one.
frame: Pass the buck to someone
nuance: Disapproving; ordinary delegation with clear responsibility is different.

meaning: Present an opposing view to test an argument.
easyEnglish: Present an opposing view to test an argument.
japanese: 議論を深めるため、あえて反対意見を述べる。
cue: Introduce a challenge to a proposal you partly support.
reply: Let me play devil's advocate: what if the supplier raises prices?
transferCue: Invite friends to examine the downside of a travel plan.
transferReply: I'll play devil's advocate and ask whether we really need a rental car.
frame: Play devil's advocate
nuance: Clarify that you are testing the idea, not necessarily expressing your own belief.

meaning: Decide what to do as events develop.
easyEnglish: Decide what to do as events develop.
japanese: あらかじめ決めすぎず、状況に応じて判断する。
cue: Suggest a flexible plan for an afternoon with uncertain weather.
reply: Let's play it by ear and see how the weather looks after lunch.
transferCue: Explain that you will decide when to leave based on traffic.
transferReply: We'll play it by ear once we hear the traffic update.
frame: Play it by ear
nuance: This planning sense differs from playing music by ear, which means without a score.

meaning: Choose an option that avoids unnecessary risk.
easyEnglish: Choose an option that avoids unnecessary risk.
japanese: 危険を避け、無難な方法を選ぶ。
cue: Suggest leaving extra time for an unfamiliar journey.
reply: Let's play it safe and take the earlier train.
transferCue: Explain why you backed up a document before editing.
transferReply: I wanted to play it safe, so I saved a separate copy.
frame: Play it safe
nuance: Can be sensible caution or excessive caution; the context determines the judgment.

phrase: put all your eggs in one basket
meaning: Depend entirely on one option, creating a risk if it fails.
easyEnglish: Depend entirely on one option, creating a risk if it fails.
japanese: 一つの選択肢だけに頼り、失敗した時の危険を大きくする。
cue: Advise a friend to apply for more than one position.
reply: Don't put all your eggs in one basket; apply to several teams.
transferCue: Suggest using several suppliers for an event.
transferReply: You put all your eggs in one basket if you rely on a single supplier.
frame: Don't put all your eggs in one basket
nuance: Often used as advice to keep alternatives available; it is not limited to money.

meaning: Firmly refuse something or insist on a limit.
easyEnglish: Firmly refuse something or insist on a limit.
japanese: きっぱりと拒否したり、自分の決めた限界を譲らず示したりする。
cue: Encourage a friend to set a firm boundary with guests.
reply: You can put your foot down about visitors staying without asking.
transferCue: Advise someone facing repeated last-minute work requests.
transferReply: It's time to put your foot down about those midnight calls.
frame: Put your foot down about something
nuance: Firm and sometimes authoritative; the literal driving sense means pressing the accelerator.

phrase: put your foot in your mouth
meaning: Say something embarrassing or unintentionally offensive.
easyEnglish: Say something embarrassing or unintentionally offensive.
japanese: うっかり気まずいことや失礼なことを言う。
cue: Warn a friend about making assumptions at a reunion.
reply: You might put your foot in your mouth if you assume everyone is married.
transferCue: Advise caution when discussing an unfamiliar situation.
transferReply: Ask what happened first so you don't put your foot in your mouth.
frame: Put your foot in your mouth
nuance: Common in American English; British English also uses put your foot in it.

meaning: Understand an unstated meaning from what is said or written.
easyEnglish: Understand an unstated meaning from what is said or written.
japanese: 言葉には直接表れていない意図を読み取る。
cue: Explain what you inferred from a cautious email.
reply: Reading between the lines, I think they want us to reduce the scope.
transferCue: Describe noticing a friend's unstated wish.
transferReply: If you read between the lines, she's asking for more time alone.
frame: Read between the lines
nuance: An inference can be wrong; check with the person before treating it as fact.

meaning: Sound familiar, even if you cannot remember the details.
easyEnglish: Sound familiar, even if you cannot remember the details.
japanese: 聞き覚えがある、何となく思い当たる。
cue: Respond to a name you may have heard before.
reply: That name rings a bell, but I can't place it.
transferCue: Ask whether a cafe's name sounds familiar.
transferReply: Does the name Harbor House ring a bell?
frame: Something rings a bell
nuance: Often qualified by vague memory; it does not mean you remember everything clearly.

meaning: Disturb a settled situation by challenging it or creating problems.
easyEnglish: Disturb a settled situation by challenging it or creating problems.
japanese: 安定している状況に波風を立てる。
cue: Explain why someone avoids disagreeing with a group.
reply: He rarely objects because he doesn't want to rock the boat.
transferCue: Explain why you raised a concern despite possible tension.
transferReply: I knew the question might rock the boat, but it needed an answer.
frame: Rock the boat
nuance: Usually focuses on disruption; sometimes challenging the situation is necessary or helpful.

meaning: A practical guide that works roughly in many situations.
easyEnglish: A practical guide that works roughly in many situations.
japanese: 多くの場合に使える、大まかな目安や経験則。
cue: Give a rough guide for choosing a plant pot.
reply: As a rule of thumb, choose a pot a little wider than the root ball.
transferCue: Offer a practical approach to packing for a short stay.
transferReply: My rule of thumb is to pack layers rather than one heavy coat.
frame: As a rule of thumb, …
nuance: An approximate guide, not a universal rule or a precise calculation.

meaning: Lose the energy or enthusiasm needed to continue.
easyEnglish: Lose the energy or enthusiasm needed to continue.
japanese: 続けるための気力や勢いがなくなる。
cue: Explain why you stopped tidying before finishing.
reply: I ran out of steam halfway through sorting the cupboard.
transferCue: Describe a discussion losing energy after several hours.
transferReply: The discussion ran out of steam after lunch.
frame: Run out of steam
nuance: Can describe people, activities or ideas losing momentum; these examples are figurative.

meaning: Avoid losing others' respect or feeling publicly embarrassed.
easyEnglish: Avoid losing others' respect or feeling publicly embarrassed.
japanese: 面目を保つ、人前で恥をかくのを避ける。
cue: Explain why you corrected a friend privately.
reply: I spoke to him privately so he could save face.
transferCue: Describe giving a team a tactful way to revise a decision.
transferReply: Calling it a trial helped the team save face when they changed course.
frame: Save face
nuance: About social dignity or reputation; it does not imply that the original choice was correct.

meaning: Deal with only a small part of a much larger subject.
easyEnglish: Deal with only a small part of a much larger subject.
japanese: 大きな話題や問題の、ほんの一部に触れるだけ。
cue: Explain the limited scope of a short introduction.
reply: This workshop only scratches the surface of the topic.
transferCue: Describe how much remains to discover in a city.
transferReply: After two days, we've barely scratched the surface of what this city offers.
frame: Scratch the surface of something
nuance: Often used with only or barely to emphasize how much remains.

meaning: Agree with someone about a subject.
easyEnglish: Agree with someone about a subject.
japanese: あることについて、意見が一致する。
cue: Explain that you and a friend disagree about planning.
reply: We don't always see eye to eye about how much to plan.
transferCue: Describe reaching agreement with a teammate.
transferReply: We finally see eye to eye on the main goal.
frame: See eye to eye with someone on / about something
nuance: Common in negative sentences; agreement on one issue does not mean identical opinions on everything.

meaning: Wait where you are or delay action until there is more information.
easyEnglish: Wait where you are or delay action until there is more information.
japanese: その場で待つ、状況が変わるまで行動を控える。
cue: Ask a friend to wait while you check an address.
reply: Sit tight while I confirm which entrance we need.
transferCue: Tell a team to wait for a supplier's response.
transferReply: We'll sit tight until the supplier confirms the delivery time.
frame: Sit tight until / while…
nuance: Informal reassurance or instruction; it can mean waiting without literally sitting.

meaning: A strong impression without clear evidence or deliberate reasoning.
easyEnglish: A strong impression without clear evidence or deliberate reasoning.
japanese: はっきりした根拠はないが、強く感じる直感。
cue: Explain why you want to check a plan again.
reply: I have a gut feeling that we've missed a step.
transferCue: Describe your early intuition about a new activity.
transferReply: I had a gut feeling that I'd enjoy pottery, and I did.
frame: Have a gut feeling that… / about something
nuance: An intuition is not proof; distinguish it from information you have checked.

meaning: Polite conversation about ordinary, low-stakes topics.
easyEnglish: Polite conversation about ordinary, low-stakes topics.
japanese: その場を和ませる、日常的な話題の軽い雑談。
cue: Explain how you began chatting with a new neighbor.
reply: We made small talk about the weather before introducing ourselves.
transferCue: Describe the opening minutes of a professional meeting.
transferReply: The meeting began with a little small talk about everyone's weekend.
frame: Make small talk about something
nuance: Usually uncountable; not the same as speaking quietly or giving a short formal talk.

meaning: Things have gone well up to this point.
easyEnglish: Things have gone well up to this point.
japanese: 今のところ順調。
cue: Give a brief update on a trial period.
reply: So far so good; the new schedule is working for everyone.
transferCue: Tell a friend how your first camping trip is going.
transferReply: So far so good, though we haven't tried cooking yet.
frame: So far so good
nuance: Leaves open how things will develop; it is not a final assessment.

meaning: Said when someone appears just as you were talking about them.
easyEnglish: Said when someone appears just as you were talking about them.
japanese: ちょうど話題にしていた人が現れた時の「噂をすれば」。
cue: Greet a friend who arrives as you mention them.
reply: Speak of the devil! We were just talking about your new job.
transferCue: React when a teammate joins a call at the right moment.
transferReply: Speak of the devil; here's Maya to tell us how it went.
frame: Speak of the devil!
nuance: Informal and usually playful; use when the person will understand the friendly intent.

meaning: Offend people by interfering with their responsibilities or interests.
easyEnglish: Offend people by interfering with their responsibilities or interests.
japanese: 人の担当や領域に踏み込み、不快にさせる。
cue: Explain why you checked responsibilities before helping.
reply: I checked who was in charge because I didn't want to step on toes.
transferCue: Describe a consultant's tactful approach to a project.
transferReply: She suggested changes carefully, without stepping on toes.
frame: Step on someone's toes
nuance: Informal; a person's possessive can appear before toes. British English also uses tread on someone's toes.

meaning: Accept a less active or less influential role.
easyEnglish: Accept a less active or less influential role.
japanese: 積極的に関わるのを控え、脇に回る。
cue: Explain that you want a colleague to lead a discussion.
reply: I'll take a back seat and let Jun lead this meeting.
transferCue: Describe becoming less involved in a club after many years.
transferReply: After five years as organizer, she decided to take a back seat.
frame: Take a back seat / take a back seat to something
nuance: With to, it can mean become less important than another priority.

meaning: Decline an invitation now while suggesting another time.
easyEnglish: Decline an invitation now while suggesting another time.
japanese: 今回は誘いを断り、別の機会にする。
cue: Decline dinner because of a prior commitment.
reply: Can I take a rain check on dinner? I'm helping my sister tonight.
transferCue: Postpone a walk because you have work to finish.
transferReply: I'd love to walk with you, but could I take a rain check until next week?
frame: Take a rain check on something
nuance: Informal; proposing another time helps show that the interest is sincere.

meaning: Decide to do something important despite nervousness or uncertainty.
easyEnglish: Decide to do something important despite nervousness or uncertainty.
japanese: 不安があっても、思い切って大きな行動に踏み出す。
cue: Say that you finally signed up for an acting course.
reply: I finally took the plunge and signed up for acting classes.
transferCue: Describe a friend opening their own small business.
transferReply: After months of planning, she took the plunge and opened the shop.
frame: Take the plunge and do something
nuance: Usually follows hesitation about a significant choice, rather than a routine action.

meaning: The advantages of two different situations combined.
easyEnglish: The advantages of two different situations combined.
japanese: 二つの異なるものの良いところを両方得ること。
cue: Describe living near nature while staying close to a city.
reply: Living by the park near the station gives us the best of both worlds.
transferCue: Explain why a flexible work arrangement suits you.
transferReply: Working partly at home and partly with the team gives me the best of both worlds.
frame: Have / get the best of both worlds
nuance: Name the two benefits so the comparison is clear.

meaning: The overall situation beyond the immediate details.
easyEnglish: The overall situation beyond the immediate details.
japanese: 目の前の細部だけではない、物事の全体像。
cue: Ask a team to consider the purpose behind a small change.
reply: Let's look at the bigger picture before arguing over one button.
transferCue: Explain why a short-term setback does not change your goal.
transferReply: In the bigger picture, this delay is only a small part of the project.
frame: Look at / consider the bigger picture
nuance: Big picture is another common form; it concerns overall context or longer-term aims.

meaning: An obvious difficult issue that people avoid discussing.
easyEnglish: An obvious difficult issue that people avoid discussing.
japanese: 誰もが気づいているのに、触れようとしない重大な問題。
cue: Raise the budget problem everyone has avoided.
reply: We need to address the elephant in the room: we don't have enough funding.
transferCue: Explain why a reunion conversation felt strained.
transferReply: Their old disagreement was the elephant in the room all evening.
frame: Address / acknowledge the elephant in the room
nuance: Use for a shared but avoided issue, not simply any large problem.

meaning: An extra benefit that makes an already good situation better.
easyEnglish: An extra benefit that makes an already good situation better.
japanese: すでに良いことに加わる、さらにうれしいおまけ。
cue: Explain how an upgrade improved an already enjoyable trip.
reply: The trip was wonderful, and the room upgrade was the icing on the cake.
transferCue: Describe an extra reward after meaningful work.
transferReply: Helping the students was rewarding; the thank-you letter was the icing on the cake.
frame: Something is the icing on the cake
nuance: Usually positive. Frosting on the cake is an American alternative.

meaning: The small visible part of a much larger issue.
easyEnglish: The small visible part of a much larger issue.
japanese: 大きな問題のうち、表に見えているほんの一部。氷山の一角。
cue: Explain that a few complaints suggest a broader problem.
reply: Those complaints may be the tip of the iceberg.
transferCue: Describe discovering that a repair involves more than expected.
transferReply: The loose tile was just the tip of the iceberg; the whole floor needed work.
frame: Something is the tip of the iceberg
nuance: Often used for problems whose full size is hidden; evidence is needed to establish that size.

meaning: During both good and difficult times.
easyEnglish: During both good and difficult times.
japanese: 良い時も悪い時も、どんな時でも。
cue: Thank a friend for consistent support over the years.
reply: You've stood by me through thick and thin.
transferCue: Describe a family's loyalty to a small local club.
transferReply: They've supported the club through thick and thin for decades.
frame: Support / stay with someone through thick and thin
nuance: Usually expresses loyalty and commitment over time.

meaning: Stop trying because you accept that you cannot succeed.
easyEnglish: Stop trying because you accept that you cannot succeed.
japanese: これ以上は無理だと認め、諦める。
cue: Explain that you are not ready to abandon a project.
reply: I'm not ready to throw in the towel after one setback.
transferCue: Describe deciding to stop an unsuccessful repair attempt.
transferReply: After three failed repairs, we threw in the towel and replaced it.
frame: Throw in the towel
nuance: Informal; implies giving up after struggle rather than finishing normally.

meaning: Uncertain, with a real risk that things may fail.
easyEnglish: Uncertain, with a real risk that things may fail.
japanese: うまくいくか危うく、予断を許さない。
cue: Describe narrowly catching the last bus.
reply: It was touch and go, but we caught the last bus.
transferCue: Explain that an event almost had to be cancelled.
transferReply: The event was touch and go until the replacement sound system arrived.
frame: It was touch and go whether…
nuance: Describes uncertainty about a successful outcome; before a noun, write touch-and-go.

meaning: Choose to ignore something you know is wrong.
easyEnglish: Choose to ignore something you know is wrong.
japanese: 問題だと知りながら、見て見ぬふりをする。
cue: Say that repeated unfair treatment must be addressed.
reply: We can't turn a blind eye to the way volunteers are being treated.
transferCue: Explain why you reported a recurring rule violation.
transferReply: I didn't want to turn a blind eye to the blocked emergency exit.
frame: Turn a blind eye to something
nuance: Implies deliberate ignoring, not simply failing to notice; use plain wording when preferred.

meaning: Start behaving in a better or more responsible way.
easyEnglish: Start behaving in a better or more responsible way.
japanese: 心を入れ替え、行いを改める。
cue: Describe your decision to stop arriving late.
reply: I'm turning over a new leaf and leaving home ten minutes earlier.
transferCue: Explain that a friend has changed an old habit.
transferReply: He's turned over a new leaf and now returns borrowed things promptly.
frame: Turn over a new leaf
nuance: Usually describes improvement in behavior rather than any new activity.

meaning: Without attracting attention or being noticed.
easyEnglish: Without attracting attention or being noticed.
japanese: 注目されたり気づかれたりせずに。
cue: Describe a small project that grew quietly.
reply: The project developed under the radar until the first public demo.
transferCue: Explain why a good film received little attention.
transferReply: That lovely documentary stayed under the radar for months.
frame: Stay / fly / operate under the radar
nuance: Can describe low visibility without implying secrecy or wrongdoing.

meaning: In an obvious or nearby place that you have failed to notice.
easyEnglish: In an obvious or nearby place that you have failed to notice.
japanese: すぐ目の前にあるのに、気づいていない。
cue: Point out a friend's keys on the table in front of them.
reply: Your keys are right under your nose, beside the mug.
transferCue: Tell a colleague that an answer was easy to find.
transferReply: The answer was under your nose in the first paragraph.
frame: Right under your nose
nuance: Can also describe something happening nearby unnoticed; it often carries surprise or mild criticism.

meaning: Still undecided or uncertain.
easyEnglish: Still undecided or uncertain.
japanese: まだ決まっていない、不確かな状態で。
cue: Explain that your holiday dates are not settled.
reply: Our holiday dates are still up in the air.
transferCue: Say that a possible event location remains uncertain.
transferReply: The venue is up in the air until we hear from the owner.
frame: Something is still up in the air
nuance: Use for unresolved plans or questions; it does not mean they have been cancelled.

meaning: Having the latest information or enough understanding to take part.
easyEnglish: Having the latest information or enough understanding to take part.
japanese: 最新の情報や必要な知識を把握して。
cue: Offer a short update to a returning colleague.
reply: I'll get you up to speed on what changed while you were away.
transferCue: Explain that a new volunteer now understands the process.
transferReply: She's up to speed with the booking system after this morning's training.
frame: Get / bring someone up to speed on something
nuance: Concerns information or practical readiness; it need not refer to literal speed.

meaning: A past problem that is no longer worth being upset about.
easyEnglish: A past problem that is no longer worth being upset about.
japanese: すでに過ぎ去り、今はもう気にしていない問題。
cue: Reassure a friend that you no longer resent an old mistake.
reply: That missed invitation is water under the bridge now.
transferCue: Explain that you and a colleague have moved beyond a disagreement.
transferReply: We've talked it through; the disagreement is water under the bridge.
frame: Something is water under the bridge
nuance: Only speak for your own feelings; another person may not consider the issue settled.

phrase: wear your heart on your sleeve
meaning: Show your feelings openly.
easyEnglish: Show your feelings openly.
japanese: 気持ちを隠さず、表に出す。
cue: Describe a friend's openly emotional reactions.
reply: You wear your heart on your sleeve; we can always tell when you're excited.
transferCue: Encourage someone who feels embarrassed about visible emotion.
transferReply: It's okay to wear your heart on your sleeve when something matters to you.
frame: Wear your heart on your sleeve
nuance: Can suggest warmth or emotional openness, not necessarily romantic feelings.

meaning: When a situation requires a firm decision or action.
easyEnglish: When a situation requires a firm decision or action.
japanese: いざという時、決断や行動が必要になった時。
cue: Explain your fallback plan if accommodation fails.
reply: When push comes to shove, we can stay with my cousin.
transferCue: Describe who will support a difficult decision.
transferReply: I think the team will support us when push comes to shove.
frame: When push comes to shove, …
nuance: Informal; often introduces what someone will really do when circumstances demand it.

meaning: Information or recommendations passed between people in conversation.
easyEnglish: Information or recommendations passed between people in conversation.
japanese: 人から人へ伝わる口コミ。
cue: Explain how customers discovered your small shop.
reply: Most customers found us through word of mouth.
transferCue: Describe how a local concert attracted an audience.
transferReply: News of the concert spread by word of mouth.
frame: By / through word of mouth
nuance: Before a noun, hyphenate: word-of-mouth recommendations.

meaning: Useful or rewarding enough to justify the time or effort.
easyEnglish: Useful or rewarding enough to justify the time or effort.
japanese: 時間や手間をかけるだけの価値がある。
cue: Recommend taking time to see a small exhibition.
reply: It's worth your while to visit the upstairs gallery.
transferCue: Explain why a friend should compare available courses.
transferReply: Comparing the course outlines will be worth your while.
frame: Be worth your while to do something
nuance: While refers to time here; worthwhile is a related one-word adjective.

meaning: A strong expression of agreement.
easyEnglish: A strong expression of agreement.
japanese: 「本当にそのとおり」と強く同意する表現。
cue: Strongly agree when a friend says a hike was tiring.
reply: You can say that again! My legs are still aching.
transferCue: Agree with a colleague who says a meeting was unusually useful.
transferReply: You can say that again; we finally have a clear plan.
frame: You can say that again!
nuance: An idiomatic response, not a request to repeat the words.

phrase: your guess is as good as mine
meaning: I do not know any more about the answer than you do.
easyEnglish: I do not know any more about the answer than you do.
japanese: 自分も同じくらい分からない。
cue: Answer a friend who asks when a delayed bus will arrive.
reply: Your guess is as good as mine; the display hasn't updated.
transferCue: Respond to speculation about an unexpected meeting.
transferReply: Your guess is as good as mine about why they called the meeting.
frame: Your guess is as good as mine
nuance: Informal; it admits shared uncertainty rather than offering an actual guess.

meaning: Something different from your usual routine or activity.
easyEnglish: Something different from your usual routine or activity.
japanese: 普段とは違う活動やペースによる気分転換。
cue: Describe enjoying a slower weekend activity.
reply: Gardening was a welcome change of pace after a week at my desk.
transferCue: Suggest trying a different kind of outing.
transferReply: A museum visit would be a nice change of pace from our usual shopping trips.
frame: A welcome / nice change of pace
nuance: Especially American English; a change can involve a different activity, not just speed.

meaning: The practical details needed to understand or do something.
easyEnglish: The practical details needed to understand or do something.
japanese: 物事を理解したり進めたりするための、実務的な基本事項。
cue: Ask to discuss how a proposal will actually work.
reply: Let's go through the nuts and bolts of running the workshop.
transferCue: Explain what an introductory course teaches.
transferReply: The course covers the nuts and bolts of managing a small shop.
frame: The nuts and bolts of something
nuance: Usually practical mechanics rather than broad goals or abstract theory.

meaning: In a difficult situation with limited options.
easyEnglish: In a difficult situation with limited options.
japanese: 選べる手段が少なく、困った状況にある。
cue: Explain why a cancelled train caused you trouble.
reply: The cancellation left us in a tight spot with no buses running.
transferCue: Ask for help covering an unexpected absence.
transferReply: We're in a tight spot with two people off; could you cover an hour?
frame: Be / put someone in a tight spot
nuance: Informal; can involve practical, social or financial difficulties.

meaning: In a situation requiring more knowledge or skill than you have.
easyEnglish: In a situation requiring more knowledge or skill than you have.
japanese: 自分の知識や能力では対応しきれない状況で。
cue: Reassure a friend struggling in an advanced class.
reply: If you feel out of your depth, you can ask to join the introductory class.
transferCue: Advise a new supervisor to seek support when needed.
transferReply: Don't hide it if you're out of your depth; ask an experienced colleague.
frame: Be / feel out of your depth
nuance: Especially British English; it describes the demands of a situation, not a person's overall worth.

meaning: Free from an obligation, blame or a difficult responsibility.
easyEnglish: Free from an obligation, blame or a difficult responsibility.
japanese: 義務や責任、困った立場から解放されて。
cue: Tell a colleague that another person can lead a session.
reply: You're off the hook for tomorrow's training; I've found another speaker.
transferCue: Explain why an apology does not remove responsibility.
transferReply: Saying sorry doesn't let us off the hook for repairing the damage.
frame: Be / let someone off the hook
nuance: Informal; the taught sense concerns responsibility, not a telephone receiver.

meaning: A rough number that is close enough for an early estimate.
easyEnglish: A rough number that is close enough for an early estimate.
japanese: 大まかな見積もりの数字。
cue: A client asks for a rough cost before you have checked every detail.
reply: I can give you a ballpark figure, but I'll need the measurements for a firm quote.
transferCue: A friend wants to know roughly how many guests to plan for.
transferReply: A ballpark figure would be forty guests, including the children.
frame: Give / ask for a ballpark figure
nuance: Informal, especially in planning and business. Make clear that the number is approximate.

meaning: Something you want to complain to someone about.
easyEnglish: Something you want to complain to someone about.
japanese: 相手に言いたい不満や文句。
cue: Your roommate borrowed your headphones without asking. Raise the issue.
reply: I've got a bone to pick with you about my headphones.
transferCue: A teammate keeps leaving your name off shared work. Ask to discuss it.
transferReply: I have a bone to pick with you about the credits on that report.
frame: Have a bone to pick with someone about something
nuance: Can sound confrontational or playfully annoyed; tone and relationship matter.

meaning: An occasion when you only just avoid something bad.
easyEnglish: An occasion when you only just avoid something bad.
japanese: 危ないところをかろうじて切り抜けたこと。
cue: You caught a falling mug before it hit the floor. React.
reply: That was a close call; the mug nearly landed on the tiles.
transferCue: You almost sent a private draft to a large mailing list. Describe it.
transferReply: Sending that draft to everyone would have been awful. It was a close call.
frame: That was a close call
nuance: This lesson teaches narrowly avoiding trouble, not a difficult choice between similar options.

meaning: Something that brings both benefits and problems.
easyEnglish: Something that brings both benefits and problems.
japanese: 良い面と悪い面の両方があるもの。
cue: Explain why working from home helps you but also makes switching off difficult.
reply: Working from home is a double-edged sword: I save time, but I work too late.
transferCue: A popular travel video brings customers and crowds to a small village. Describe the effect.
transferReply: That publicity is a double-edged sword for the village.
frame: Something is a double-edged sword
nuance: Use for opposing effects of the same thing, not simply two unrelated disadvantages.

meaning: A situation where the rules or boundaries are not clear.
easyEnglish: A situation where the rules or boundaries are not clear.
japanese: 規則や判断の境界がはっきりしない領域。
cue: Your team has no clear policy on using personal devices. Explain the uncertainty.
reply: Using personal tablets for work is still a grey area in our policy.
transferCue: Friends disagree about whether reserving empty seats is acceptable. Describe the issue.
transferReply: Saving seats at that cafe seems to be a grey area.
frame: Something is a grey area
nuance: Gray area is the usual US spelling. It describes unclear boundaries, not necessarily wrongdoing.

meaning: An excellent place or thing that few people know about.
easyEnglish: An excellent place or thing that few people know about.
japanese: あまり知られていない、すばらしい場所やもの。
cue: Recommend a tiny bakery away from the busy main street.
reply: That bakery behind the station is a hidden gem.
transferCue: You found a little-known film you loved. Recommend it.
transferReply: The film barely got any publicity, but it's a hidden gem.
frame: A place / thing is a hidden gem
nuance: Often used in recommendations. It does not mean the place is literally hidden.

meaning: A decision to trust something without knowing that it will work.
easyEnglish: A decision to trust something without knowing that it will work.
japanese: 確信がないまま信じて踏み出すこと。
cue: Explain why joining a brand-new company felt risky.
reply: Joining a team with no finished product took a leap of faith.
transferCue: You booked a trip with someone you barely knew. Describe that decision.
transferReply: Planning a month of travel together was a leap of faith, but we got along well.
frame: Take / make a leap of faith
nuance: It emphasizes trust despite uncertainty; it does not guarantee a good result.

meaning: A situation where everyone has a fair chance under the same conditions.
easyEnglish: A situation where everyone has a fair chance under the same conditions.
japanese: 誰もが公平な条件で競争できる状況。
cue: Ask for all applicants to receive the interview questions at the same time.
reply: We need a level playing field, so everyone should get the instructions together.
transferCue: Explain why a club lends equipment to beginners.
transferReply: Lending equipment helps create a level playing field for new members.
frame: Create / provide a level playing field
nuance: A metaphor for fair opportunities, not a promise that everyone will achieve the same outcome.

meaning: A good aspect of an otherwise disappointing situation.
easyEnglish: A good aspect of an otherwise disappointing situation.
japanese: 悪い状況の中に見いだせる良い面。
cue: Your flight was cancelled, but you got an extra evening with your sister. Reflect.
reply: There was a silver lining: I got to have dinner with my sister.
transferCue: A delayed renovation gave you time to rethink the layout. Describe the benefit.
transferReply: The delay had a silver lining; we spotted a problem with the kitchen plan.
frame: A situation has a silver lining
nuance: Offer perspective gently. Pointing out a benefit too soon can sound dismissive of someone's distress.

meaning: A step that may lead to a series of increasingly harmful choices.
easyEnglish: A step that may lead to a series of increasingly harmful choices.
japanese: 悪い方向へ次々と進むきっかけになりかねないこと。
cue: You worry that making one small exception will lead to many more. Explain.
reply: Ignoring this rule could be a slippery slope toward making exceptions for everyone.
transferCue: A friend keeps reducing their sleep to finish extra work. Express concern.
transferReply: Skipping sleep whenever you're busy sounds like a slippery slope.
frame: Something is / could be a slippery slope
nuance: Usually expresses a concern about what might follow; the chain of consequences is not certain.

meaning: A long or difficult search that leads nowhere.
easyEnglish: A long or difficult search that leads nowhere.
japanese: 成果のない無駄な捜索や追跡。
cue: An outdated address sent you across town to a shop that had closed. Describe your trip.
reply: That old listing sent us on a wild goose chase.
transferCue: A wrong file name made your colleague search several archives. Apologize.
transferReply: Sorry I sent you on a wild goose chase with the wrong file name.
frame: Send someone on / go on a wild goose chase
nuance: The search is pointless or based on a false lead, not merely time-consuming.

meaning: An event that makes you realize something needs to change.
easyEnglish: An event that makes you realize something needs to change.
japanese: 何かを変える必要に気づかせる出来事。
cue: Losing an unsaved document made you start keeping backups. Explain.
reply: Losing that draft was a wake-up call about saving my work.
transferCue: Your club almost cancelled an event because too few people helped. Reflect.
transferReply: The near-cancellation was a wake-up call for everyone in the club.
frame: Something is a wake-up call for someone
nuance: This figurative sense means a warning or realization; a hotel wake-up call is literal.

meaning: A feeling of relief when a worry or responsibility is removed.
easyEnglish: A feeling of relief when a worry or responsibility is removed.
japanese: 心配や責任がなくなり、肩の荷が下りること。
cue: A friend finally finishes a stressful move. Ask how they feel.
reply: Having the move finished must be a weight off your shoulders.
transferCue: Your teammate has found someone to cover a difficult shift. Respond.
transferReply: Knowing the shift is covered should be a weight off your shoulders.
frame: Be / take a weight off someone's shoulders
nuance: Change your to my, her or another possessive when needed. Both examples address the listener.

meaning: A situation that is very different and needs a different approach.
easyEnglish: A situation that is very different and needs a different approach.
japanese: 事情が大きく変わり、別の対応が必要な状況。
cue: Your small project suddenly needs to serve thousands of people. Explain the change.
reply: Supporting thousands of users is a whole new ball game.
transferCue: Explain how cooking for a large party differs from making dinner for two.
transferReply: Cooking for thirty guests is a whole new ball game.
frame: Something is a whole new ball game
nuance: Informal. The difference is substantial, not just one small adjustment.

meaning: What people do shows their intentions more clearly than what they say.
easyEnglish: What people do shows their intentions more clearly than what they say.
japanese: 言葉より行動のほうが、その人の本心をよく示す。
cue: A friend keeps promising to help but never turns up. Explain what matters to you.
reply: Actions speak louder than words; I'd like to see him actually show up.
transferCue: Your team wants to prove it welcomes feedback. Encourage a practical response.
transferReply: Actions speak louder than words, so let's fix the problems people reported.
frame: Actions speak louder than words
nuance: A saying used to emphasize follow-through. It can sound critical after repeated promises.

meaning: Unexpectedly and very quickly.
easyEnglish: Unexpectedly and very quickly.
japanese: 突然、思いがけず。
cue: Describe an unexpected change in the weather during a walk.
reply: All of a sudden, the wind picked up and we had to turn back.
transferCue: Your quiet cafe suddenly became busy. Tell a coworker what happened.
transferReply: All of a sudden, three big groups came through the door.
frame: All of a sudden, something happened
nuance: A fixed expression: use a sudden, not the sudden.

meaning: A person whose feelings or thoughts are easy to understand.
easyEnglish: A person whose feelings or thoughts are easy to understand.
japanese: 考えや感情が表に出ていて、分かりやすい人。
cue: Your family instantly noticed that you had good news. Explain why.
reply: I'm an open book; everyone could tell I was excited.
transferCue: Describe a friend who never manages to hide disappointment.
transferReply: He's an open book, so I knew the result had upset him.
frame: Someone is an open book
nuance: It refers to easy-to-read feelings or character, not necessarily sharing every private detail.

meaning: Extremely slowly.
easyEnglish: Extremely slowly.
japanese: 非常にゆっくりと。
cue: Explain why you are late after sitting in traffic.
reply: Traffic was moving at a snail's pace near the bridge.
transferCue: A large file has barely uploaded. Describe the progress.
transferReply: This upload is crawling along at a snail's pace.
frame: Move / progress at a snail's pace
nuance: Usually expresses impatience. Keep the possessive in snail's.

meaning: At almost the last possible moment.
easyEnglish: At almost the last possible moment.
japanese: 期限や決定の直前、土壇場で。
cue: A venue became available just before you cancelled an event. Explain.
reply: We found another venue at the eleventh hour.
transferCue: Your application was nearly late. Describe when you submitted it.
transferReply: I finally submitted the application at the eleventh hour.
frame: Do something at the eleventh hour
nuance: A slightly dramatic expression. It is not a literal reference to eleven o'clock.

meaning: So worried or frustrated that you do not know what to do next.
easyEnglish: So worried or frustrated that you do not know what to do next.
japanese: どうすればよいか分からず、困り果てて。
cue: A friend has tried everything to stop a persistent leak. Acknowledge their frustration.
reply: You must be at your wits' end after all those failed repairs.
transferCue: A parent has spent hours trying to organize a cancelled school trip. Offer support.
transferReply: If you're at your wits' end with the arrangements, I can make some calls.
frame: Be at someone's wits' end
nuance: Use my wits' end for yourself. The plural possessive wits' is the conventional written form.

meaning: Recovered enough to manage normally again after illness or difficulty.
easyEnglish: Recovered enough to manage normally again after illness or difficulty.
japanese: 病気や困難から回復して、また普通にやっていける状態で。
cue: Welcome a friend who has returned after being ill.
reply: It's good to see you back on your feet and enjoying your walks again.
transferCue: Your sibling has settled into a new job after a difficult period. Encourage them.
transferReply: I'm glad you're back on your feet after such a rough year.
frame: Be / get back on someone's feet
nuance: Can describe health or a return to independence after a setback; it need not involve standing.

meaning: Finish something before the available time runs out.
easyEnglish: Finish something before the available time runs out.
japanese: 時間切れになる前にやり遂げる。
cue: Your group finished an escape-room puzzle with seconds left. Celebrate.
reply: We managed to beat the clock with just ten seconds left.
transferCue: A team needs to finish packing before the courier arrives. Encourage them.
transferReply: If we split the boxes between us, we can beat the clock.
frame: Try to / manage to beat the clock
nuance: Emphasizes working against a time limit, rather than defeating another person.

meaning: Unfairly hurtful or personal.
easyEnglish: Unfairly hurtful or personal.
japanese: 不当に相手を傷つける、卑劣な。
cue: Someone attacks a coworker's private life during a work disagreement. Object.
reply: That comment about her family was below the belt.
transferCue: A friend apologizes for a cruel joke. Explain why it bothered you.
transferReply: I can take a joke, but that one was below the belt.
frame: A remark / attack is below the belt
nuance: A boxing metaphor for an unfair personal attack. It is stronger than simply impolite.

meaning: Apply a rule less strictly to allow an exception.
easyEnglish: Apply a rule less strictly to allow an exception.
japanese: 規則を柔軟に解釈して例外を認める。
cue: A library lets a stranded visitor stay a few minutes after closing. Explain.
reply: The librarian agreed to bend the rules while we waited for our ride.
transferCue: Your club wants to accept a late entry from a new member. Discuss it.
transferReply: Could we bend the rules just this once and accept her entry?
frame: Bend the rules for someone / just this once
nuance: Usually means a limited exception; it may still be unfair, so the context matters.

meaning: Stop yourself from saying something you want to say.
easyEnglish: Stop yourself from saying something you want to say.
japanese: 言いたいことをぐっとこらえる。
cue: A friend nearly interrupts a toast with a critical comment. Advise restraint.
reply: You may need to bite your tongue until the toast is over.
transferCue: A colleague wants to correct a tiny mistake during a tense conversation. Suggest waiting.
transferReply: Sometimes it's better to bite your tongue and choose a calmer moment.
frame: Bite your tongue rather than say something
nuance: The figurative sense is deliberate restraint. Literally biting your tongue is an injury.

meaning: Do something that has not been done before in a particular area.
easyEnglish: Do something that has not been done before in a particular area.
japanese: ある分野で新しいことを切り開く。
cue: Describe a research team's genuinely new approach to a problem.
reply: Their method could break new ground in how we reuse these materials.
transferCue: Your theatre group has never staged an outdoor production. Describe the ambition.
transferReply: We want to break new ground for the company with this outdoor show.
frame: Break new ground in a field / with an approach
nuance: Can mean new for a particular group or field. Avoid using it for a routine small update.

meaning: Earn the money needed to support a household.
easyEnglish: Earn the money needed to support a household.
japanese: 生活を支えるためのお金を稼ぐ。
cue: Explain how you supported the household while your partner studied.
reply: While my partner studied, I worked evenings to bring home the bacon.
transferCue: A friend is considering turning a hobby into their main income. Be realistic.
transferReply: I love making pottery, but it doesn't bring home the bacon yet.
frame: Bring home the bacon
nuance: Informal and sometimes humorous. It is not limited to any gender or family role.

meaning: Work or study until very late at night.
easyEnglish: Work or study until very late at night.
japanese: 夜遅くまで仕事や勉強をする。
cue: Explain why you are tired after preparing a talk.
reply: I had to burn the midnight oil to get the slides ready.
transferCue: A friend has a big exam next week and is studying late. Describe their week.
transferReply: She's been burning the midnight oil for her final exam.
frame: Burn the midnight oil to do something
nuance: Describes late-night effort; it does not imply that losing sleep is a good habit.

meaning: Agree to stop a quarrel and be on friendly terms again.
easyEnglish: Agree to stop a quarrel and be on friendly terms again.
japanese: 争いをやめて仲直りする。
cue: You and a friend have been arguing over an old misunderstanding. Suggest reconciliation.
reply: Let's bury the hatchet and stop bringing up that argument.
transferCue: Two neighbors finally agreed to get along. Describe the outcome.
transferReply: They decided to bury the hatchet after talking over coffee.
frame: Bury the hatchet with someone
nuance: Usually suggests both sides ending a dispute, not simply hiding anger.

meaning: Not nearly or not at all, when used with a negative statement.
easyEnglish: Not nearly or not at all, when used with a negative statement.
japanese: 否定文で、到底〜ではない、少しも〜ではない。
cue: Someone assumes your project is nearly finished. Correct them.
reply: We're not finished by a long shot; the testing hasn't even started.
transferCue: A friend thinks the first apartment you visited was the cheapest. Disagree.
transferReply: That wasn't the cheapest place by a long shot.
frame: Not ... by a long shot
nuance: Especially common in negative statements. A long shot by itself means an unlikely attempt.

meaning: Generally, considering the situation as a whole.
easyEnglish: Generally, considering the situation as a whole.
japanese: 全体としては、概して。
cue: Give an overall view of a trip that had a few minor problems.
reply: By and large, the trip went smoothly despite a couple of delays.
transferCue: Summarize the response to your team's new schedule.
transferReply: People seem happy with the new schedule, by and large.
frame: By and large, ...
nuance: Allows for exceptions. It does not mean absolutely everyone or every time.

meaning: Discovered while actually doing something wrong.
easyEnglish: Discovered while actually doing something wrong.
japanese: 悪いことをしている現場を押さえられて。
cue: You were seen eating the cake saved for tomorrow. Admit it lightly.
reply: I was caught red-handed with a fork in the birthday cake.
transferCue: A player was seen looking at another person's cards. Describe the incident.
transferReply: He was caught red-handed looking at the cards under the table.
frame: Be caught red-handed doing something
nuance: Often used for wrongdoing, but also jokingly for minor mischief. Avoid treating a suspicion as proof.

phrase: cross that bridge when we come to it
meaning: Deal with a possible problem when it actually arises.
easyEnglish: Deal with a possible problem when it actually arises.
japanese: まだ起きていない問題は、そのときになって考える。
